cards.front: What structural abnormalities affect the reeler mouse cerebellum?
cards.back: It is small and poorly folded, with Purkinje cells clumped instead of arranged in a single layer.
cards.quote: Purkinje cells, the large output neurons of the cerebellum, left in clumps instead of a neat single layer.

cards.front: In the cerebral cortex, {{c1::superficial}} means near the pial surface.
cards.quote: Superficial means near the pial surface, the outside of the brain.
cards.section: How a normal cortex is stacked

cards.front: How does splitting the preplate establish the developing cortical plate?
cards.back: Incoming neurons divide the preplate into an upper marginal zone and a lower subplate. The neurons between them form the cortical plate.
cards.quote: The next neurons move into the middle of that sheet and split it in two:
cards.section: How a normal cortex is stacked

cards.front: Why is development of the neocortical plate by radially migrating excitatory neurons described as inside-out?
cards.back: Later-born neurons pass earlier waves and settle closer to the surface, leaving early-born neurons deep and late-born neurons superficial.
cards.quote: Each later wave climbs past the waves before it and settles just under the marginal zone.
cards.section: How a normal cortex is stacked

cards.front: Two cohorts of radially migrating excitatory neurons of the neocortical plate are labelled at different birth dates in normal development. What relative depths should they occupy as adults, and why?
cards.back: The later-born cohort should be more superficial, because each later wave passes the neurons born before it during inside-out cortical development.
cards.quote: So early-born neurons end up deep and late-born neurons end up superficial.
cards.section: How a normal cortex is stacked

cards.front: For neuronal birthdating, tritiated thymidine labels cells that are {{c1::copying DNA}}.
cards.quote: A radioactive building block of DNA, tritiated thymidine, labels cells that are copying DNA.

cards.front: In a thymidine birthdating experiment, take a labelled cell’s initial label as 100%. If label is roughly halved at each division, what percentage remains per descendant after three further divisions?
cards.back: Remaining label ≈ 100% × (1/2)^3 = 12.5% of the initial label per descendant.
cards.quote: Cells that keep dividing after the pulse dilute the label by roughly half at each division.

cards.front: A cortical mutant has the normal neuronal classes and birth schedule, but labelled cohorts settle at different depths from controls. What developmental defect does this support?
cards.back: A placement defect: the same classes are generated on schedule, but their final positions differ.
cards.quote: Right neurons in the wrong place would show up as the same classes, born on the same schedule, ending at different depths.

cards.front: Why must a neuronal birthdating study identify labelled cell types as well as record their positions?
cards.back: The label gives birth date, not cell class. Identifying types is needed to determine whether corresponding classes occupy different positions.
cards.quote: The label gives the birth date; the class comes from identifying each labelled neuron's type.

cards.front: How does birth order relate to final depth in reeler neocortex?
cards.back: Early-born neurons tend to be superficial and late-born neurons deep, with substantial scatter rather than a clean mirror image of normal cortex.
cards.quote: Real reeler cortex shows an inverted trend with a lot of scatter, not a clean mirror image.

cards.front: Why does reeler cortex retain a superplate above the cortical plate?
cards.back: The preplate fails to split. Incoming cortical plate neurons pile up beneath it, leaving subplate and Cajal-Retzius cells together above them.
cards.quote: Later work showed where it starts to go wrong: in reeler the preplate fails to split.

cards.front: The main source of Reelin in developing mouse cortex is the {{c1::Cajal-Retzius cells}} in the marginal zone.
cards.quote: CR-50 that stained Cajal-Retzius cells in the marginal zone.

cards.front: CR-50 recognizes Reelin. Adding it to reassembling embryonic cortical cultures makes normal tissue organize like reeler tissue. What role for Reelin does this support?
cards.back: Reelin is needed for normal organization in this culture assay. Disrupting its function reproduces the organizational defect; the assay does not establish what spatial message it carries.
cards.quote: Added to cultures in which embryonic cortical cells reassemble, it made normal tissue organize like reeler tissue.

cards.front: A protein that lacks enzyme activity and links other proteins together is an {{c1::adaptor}}.
cards.quote: a protein with no enzyme activity of its own that links one protein to others

cards.front: What genetic relationship links the scrambler and yotari mouse mutants?
cards.back: They are two alleles of Dab1, which encodes an adaptor in the Reelin pathway.
cards.quote: both turned out to be mutations in Dab1 (Disabled-1), so they are two alleles of one gene.

cards.front: Which receptor pair is partly redundant in the mouse Reelin pathway?
cards.back: ApoER2 and VLDLR. Loss of both gives a brain close to reeler; either single knockout is milder.
cards.quote: ApoER2 and VLDLR, have a brain close to reeler, while either single knockout is milder.

cards.front: For two receptors serving one signal, why can losing either alone cause a mild defect while losing both causes a severe defect?
cards.back: Their functions partly overlap. The remaining receptor can transmit some signal after a single loss; the double loss removes that backup.
cards.quote: The receptor leg has two runners whose jobs partly overlap.

cards.front: Why do similar loss-of-function phenotypes suggest a shared signaling pathway, and what can they not establish?
cards.back: Losing different essential steps of one relay can block the same output. Similar phenotypes suggest a shared pathway but do not establish the order of its components.
cards.quote: Nor do matching phenotypes give the order of the runners.

cards.front: Why can a change in one signaling protein’s steady-state level after deleting another protein fail to establish their pathway order?
cards.back: Feedback from a later step can change an earlier component. A steady-state difference alone does not establish which acts first.
cards.quote: a changed steady state alone cannot give the order, because a later step can feed back on an earlier one.

cards.front: How does extracellular Reelin activate Dab1 in the developing mouse cortex?
cards.back: Reelin binds ApoER2 and VLDLR; the Src-family kinases Fyn and Src phosphorylate Dab1 on tyrosine, enabling it to recruit effectors.
cards.quote: Reelin (from Cajal-Retzius cells) → binds ApoER2 and VLDLR → Fyn and Src phosphorylate Dab1 on tyrosine → phospho-Dab1 recruits effectors

cards.front: Adding Reelin to cultured neurons rapidly increases Dab1 tyrosine phosphorylation. Binding studies show Reelin binds ApoER2 and VLDLR directly. What pathway order does this support?
cards.back: Reelin acts through the receptors upstream of Dab1 activation. The acute response helps establish direction beyond what steady-state protein levels alone can show.
cards.quote: Reelin binds ApoER2 and VLDLR directly and that this binding leads to tyrosine phosphorylation of Dab1.

cards.front: Why can Reelin-deficient brains contain more Dab1 protein but less phosphorylated Dab1?
cards.back: Reelin normally promotes Dab1 phosphorylation. Phosphorylated Dab1 is targeted for destruction, so poorly phosphorylated Dab1 probably degrades less efficiently and accumulates.
cards.quote: with no Reelin, Dab1 is poorly phosphorylated, so it is probably degraded less efficiently and builds up.

cards.front: A mouse cortical neuron has normal Reelin receptors but Dab1 cannot be phosphorylated at its signaling tyrosines. What positioning defect is expected, and why?
cards.back: A reeler-like positioning defect is expected: the receptors can receive Reelin, but Dab1 cannot pass the signal onward through its phosphorylation-dependent step.
cards.quote: Fyn and Src phosphorylate Dab1 on tyrosine → phospho-Dab1 recruits effectors

cards.front: Phosphorylated Dab1 is marked for destruction by a ubiquitin ligase built on {{c1::Cullin 5}}.
cards.quote: Phosphorylated Dab1 is marked by a ubiquitin ligase built on Cullin 5 and destroyed

cards.front: Cullin 5 is reduced in migrating mouse cortical neurons. What happens to their positioning, and why?
cards.back: They migrate too far and pile up at the top of the cortical plate, because impaired shut-off allows active Dab1 to accumulate.
cards.quote: Active Dab1 built up and the neurons migrated too far, piling up at the top of the cortical plate.

cards.front: Why does the combined evidence from Reelin loss and Cullin 5 knockdown argue against treating more active Dab1 as always better for cortical positioning?
cards.back: Reelin loss reduces Dab1 activation and disrupts placement; Cullin 5 knockdown lets active Dab1 accumulate and neurons overshoot. The governing rule is that positioning needs both activation and shut-off, so more active Dab1 does not always improve placement.
cards.quote: Normal positioning needs both the signal and its shut-off.

cards.front: How does a permissive developmental signal differ from an instructive one?
cards.back: A permissive signal allows an outcome chosen by something else; an instructive signal specifies the outcome itself.
cards.quote: A permissive signal allows an outcome that something else chooses; an instructive signal chooses the outcome itself.
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: Why does loss of a developmental outcome after removing a signal fail to show that the signal is instructive?
cards.back: Both permissive and instructive signals can be necessary. Removal establishes a requirement but does not show whether the signal specifies the outcome.
cards.quote: Removal shows that a signal is needed, not what it says.
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: A migrating cell is proposed to read a secreted signal as a simple attractant. Move the source behind the cell. What movement is predicted, and why?
cards.back: The cell should turn toward the relocated source, because a simple attractant conveys direction through where the signal is located.
cards.quote: One test of a spatial message is to keep the signal present while changing where it is.
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: Reelin supplied from the ventricular zone rescues preplate splitting in reeler mice, but neurons do not migrate down toward that source. Which simple model is challenged?
cards.back: A simple come-here attractant model is challenged: the relocated source supports some development without drawing neurons toward it. The rescue is partial and does not identify the actual cue.
cards.quote: It rescued preplate splitting and the ataxia (the unsteady walk), but not every defect. Neurons did not migrate down toward the source.
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: In developing mouse cortex, an ectopic Reelin spot gathers leading processes and becomes surrounded by neuronal cell bodies; later-born neurons pass earlier ones toward its center. What does this establish about Reelin location?
cards.back: A local Reelin source can organize an inside-out arrangement. This shows location can matter, but does not establish that the normal cortical cue is a gradient.
cards.quote: This built a small inside-out arrangement around the source. Location clearly mattered there.
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: Bathing embryonic reeler cortical slices in Reelin improves cortical plate organization. Why does this neither exclude local attraction nor demonstrate normal layering across many waves?
cards.back: The assay shows rescue without a source at the top. By the stated rule that Reelin can concentrate on matrix and cell surfaces, even medium need not mean even tissue exposure. The short-term assay also did not measure layering across many waves.
cards.quote: Even supply in the medium is not proof of even supply in the tissue, though:
cards.section: Needed, but what does it say?

cards.front: What is the multipolar phase of a typical later-born, radially migrating excitatory neuron of the neocortex?
cards.back: A phase with several short processes, wandering in the intermediate zone below the cortical plate before orienting toward the surface.
cards.quote: it has several short processes, wanders in the intermediate zone below the cortical plate, and is not yet oriented toward the surface.

cards.front: How does final somal translocation differ from climbing a radial glial fiber?
cards.back: The neuron anchors its leading process in the marginal zone and pulls its cell body upward without using the glial fiber.
cards.quote: it anchors its leading process in the marginal zone and pulls its cell body up behind it.

cards.front: Which two migration stages are linked to Reelin signaling through Dab1 and Rap1 in mouse cortex?
cards.back: Multipolar neuron orientation toward the cortical plate, involving N-cadherin, and final somal translocation, again involving changes in adhesion.
cards.quote: Reelin signalling through Dab1 and the small GTPase Rap1 has been linked to two of these stages.

cards.front: Suppose a migration signal changes adhesion only at particular developmental stages. Two cells at different stages receive the same signal. Must they move identically, and why?
cards.back: No. Their responses can differ because the same adhesion signal acts in the context of each cell’s developmental stage.
cards.quote: what it does depends on the neuron's stage.

cards.front: How would you test whether a focal Reelin source attracts migrating cortical neurons rather than simply stopping them on contact?
cards.back: In Reelin-deficient tissue, relocate a focal source and track labelled neurons while measuring the Reelin distribution. The stated models predict turning toward a source for attraction, versus halting without turning for stopping. Loss of the response without Dab1 or both receptors would support pathway dependence.
cards.quote: The focal half, tracking neurons' paths while measuring where the Reelin is, would be the stronger test of attraction.

cards.front: Migrating neurons encounter a focal signal without turning toward it. What behavior would distinguish a detachment response from a simple stop response?
cards.back: Leaving the glial fiber and potentially moving another way supports detachment; halting at the signal without that release supports a simple stop response.
cards.quote: Neurons leave their glial fiber there, without turning, and may move on another way.

cards.front: Reelin improves reeler slice organization, but receptor-activating antibodies increase Dab1 phosphorylation without correcting organization. What does this show about the phosphorylation readout?
cards.back: Dab1 phosphorylation alone is insufficient for this rescue. By the distinction between pathway activation and the migration outcome, a biochemical readout cannot substitute for measuring tissue organization; the result does not identify which additional feature is required.
cards.quote: antibodies that activated the receptors raised Dab1 phosphorylation but did not correct the reeler phenotype.

cards.front: Reelin can rescue some defects from below the cortex, organize neurons around a local spot, and improve slices when supplied in medium. What common interpretation fits without choosing a single spatial command?
cards.back: A stage-dependent adhesion switch can fit all three: the normal source is not always required, yet local signal can organize responding neurons. This rests on Reelin’s links to orientation and somal translocation; it leaves gradient, boundary and permissive-state models unresolved.
cards.quote: Separate experiments on single neurons fit, without proving, the view that Reelin acts at particular stages, partly through adhesion.

cards.front: One model links terminal translocation to neuronal alpha5beta1 integrin activation. Yet removing beta1 integrin from mouse neurons produces no major layering defects. What does this imply about whether that step is essential?
cards.back: That integrin step may not be essential for layering. The model links terminal translocation to alpha5beta1-mediated adhesion, but the loss-of-function result weakens an essential-role claim; it does not exclude an adhesion-based contribution.
cards.quote: removing beta1 integrin from mouse neurons does not cause major layering defects, so this step may not be essential.
cards.section: An integrin model for the last step

cards.front: What developmental brain disorder can rare recessive RELN mutations cause in humans?
cards.back: Lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia: a thick, smooth or nearly smooth cortex with few broad folds, and a small cerebellum.
cards.quote: In humans, rare recessive RELN mutations cause lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia,
